# Diagnosing a Dashcam Blown Car Fuse: Why Your Vehicle's Electrical System Is Tripping

You recently installed a dashcam on your 2010 Chevy Equinox, only to find that plugging the charger into the front cigarette lighter port caused all three 12V ports in the vehicle to fail. After replacing the fuses, the issue returned within two hours of re-plugging the device. This isn't just a "bad part" scenario; it is a classic electrical fault requiring systematic diagnosis. When a single accessory blows every fuse in a vehicle's circuit, the root cause is almost certainly a short circuit or an undervoltage lockout (UVLO) event that the car's Battery Management System interprets as a catastrophic failure.

The most critical step before assuming the dashcam unit itself is defective is to isolate the power source from the load. You mentioned wanting to test the charging unit and USB cable separately. This is the correct approach, but standard multimeter checks can be misleading if you are not looking for specific voltage signatures under load.

### Isolating the Short Circuit

To verify if the charger or cable is defective, you need to measure resistance with the power disconnected. If your charger uses a barrel jack (the round plug), inspect the internal barrel connector. A common failure point in these units is a loose spring contact or a frized solder joint where the barrel meets the PCB. If the internal diode bridge on the charger's side has shorted, it will draw massive current immediately upon connection, regardless of the USB cable's condition.

Connect your multimeter to the input pins of the car charger (the barrel jack side) and set it to measure resistance. You should see a high impedance reading (usually > 10kÎ©). If you measure near-zero ohms at the input, the charger has shorted internally and must be replaced. Do not rely on visual inspection alone; the internal capacitors can remain charged even when unplugged, though this is rare in modern switching power supplies.

Once you confirm the charger and cable are healthy, the fault lies within the dashcam's power management logic or its internal circuitry. The fact that all three fuses blew suggests a massive current draw exceeding the fuse rating (typically 15A to 20A for automotive circuits). This usually happens when the device attempts to start up but encounters a dead short on its internal rail, triggering the car's safety mechanism to cut power instantly.

### The Undervoltage Lockout Trap

There is a second, often overlooked cause: the undervoltage lockout (UVLO) feature found in many dashcams designed for hardwiring. These devices are programmed to shut down if the battery voltage drops below a certain threshold (often around 11.8V or 12V) to prevent deep discharge of the car's battery.

However, some cheaper implementations of this logic have a flaw: they attempt to restart automatically once the voltage recovers slightly, creating a "click-clack" cycle. If your dashcam has a UVLO feature and you are plugging it into a port that shares a fuse with other accessories, the initial surge or the repeated restart attempts can cause thermal runaway in the fuse if the current spikes too high.

To rule this out, disconnect the USB cable from the car charger entirely. Plug only the barrel jack into the cigarette lighter. If the fuse blows immediately without connecting to the camera head, the short is definitely inside the charger's barrel connection or the car's port itself. If the fuse holds with just the barrel jack plugged in but blows when you connect the USB side, the fault is inside the dashcam's USB input circuitry.

### Hardwiring vs. Cigarette Lighter

If you confirm the hardware is sound but still experience issues, consider how you power the device. Using a hardwire kit (tapping directly into the fuse box or running a wire to the battery) is often superior for dashcams that need 24/7 recording. However, hardwiring requires careful attention to gauge matching and proper fusing.

If you proceed with hardwiring, ensure you are using an inline fuse holder rated correctly for the wire gauge (e.g., a 10A or 15A blade fuse). If you tap into a factory accessory fuse that is already near its limit, adding another load can push it over the edge. A common mistake is tapping into a fuse labeled "ACC" and expecting it to handle the dashcam's startup surge without realizing the total amperage now exceeds the fuse rating.

Alternatively, if you stick with the cigarette lighter method, ensure you are using a high-quality charger that includes a soft-start feature. Cheap chargers often have no current limiting at turn-on, causing an inrush current spike that can blow fuses even if the device is otherwise functional. Look for chargers with active PTC resettable fuses or explicit "soft start" circuitry to mitigate this risk.

Before abandoning the unit, take it to a local electronics repair shop. They can bench-test the input voltage and check for shorts on the internal rails without risking your vehicle's electrical system further. If the dashcam has a known UVLO issue, you may need to modify the firmware or hardware to bypass it, but this requires specific knowledge of the device's board layout.
